summaries.summary: Accurate g2p matters for text-to-speech and automatic speech recognition, but most languages lack extensive pronunciation data, so high resource data may enable low resource g2p.
The authors treat g2p as multisource NMT from standard orthography to IPA, with a shared encoder–decoder exploiting orthographic and phonemic similarities.
deri2016grapheme adapted high resource wFST models to low resource languages using language and phoneme distance metrics computed from Phoible and URIEL.
Other low resource g2p systems combined multiple models, including phoneme-level voting and recurrent neural networks combined with wFST-based Phonetisaurus.
kim2012universal used supervised learning with an undirected graphical model, naïve grapheme-to-IPA mappings, and phonotactic features that outperformed WALS features.
Google's zero-shot neural machine translation system shares an encoder and decoder, uses target-language tokens, and inspires the g2p system's source-language tokens and single IPA target.
Other multilingually-trained neural networks include phoneme-level polyglot language models and ostling2017continuous, but neither was applied to g2p.
g2p converts a word's orthographic representation into a phonemic representation, where phonemes are abstract sound units with context-dependent realizations.
Writing systems usually do not distinguish allophones, and English writes both sounds as INLINEFORM0 p INLINEFORM1, unlike Hindi and Eastern Armenian.
Most writing systems are glottographic, but graphemes rarely correspond one-to-one with phonemes, as multiple graphemes can represent one phoneme.
A single grapheme can represent multiple phonemes, such as in syllabaries where each symbol represents a syllable.
Many languages have silent letters, as in the word hora in Spanish.
More complicated correspondences include silent e in English affecting the previous vowel, as in cape and cap.
Orthographic systems can have these phenomena while remaining unambiguous, but some contain ambiguities, including English spelling and Arabic and Hebrew abjads.
Consequently, g2p is harder than replacing each grapheme symbol with a corresponding phoneme symbol and replaces a grapheme sequence INLINEFORM0.
g2p replaces a grapheme sequence with a phoneme sequence INLINEFORM0.
Data-driven g2p finds the phoneme sequence maximizing the likelihood of the grapheme sequence, where sequences are not necessarily the same length.
Data-driven approaches suit complex rules, ambiguous orthographies, and multilingual g2p, making a data-driven sequence-to-sequence model a natural choice.
The authors use a neural encoder–decoder model with attention, where the encoder compresses a source grapheme sequence and the decoder generates a phoneme sequence.
The encoder and decoder are recurrent neural networks trained jointly, with a bidirectional encoder, long short-term memory units, and luong2015effective general global attention.
All models were implemented with OpenNMT, and hyperparameters determined by experimentation are listed in Table TABREF8.
To handle different pronunciation patterns, each grapheme sequence is prepended with an artificial token containing the language's ISO 639-3 code in angle brackets.
The English word `real' is presented as INLINEFORM0 eng INLINEFORM1 r e a l.
The artificial token is treated as a grapheme sequence element, unlike johnson2016google's target-language tokens and ostling2017continuous's language embeddings.
The authors use deri2016grapheme's multilingual Wiktionary pronunciation corpus, partitioned into training and test sets, instead of the monolingual Carnegie Mellon Pronouncing Dictionary.
The corpus provides automatically cleaned IPA transcriptions aligned with Phoible inventories, but cleaning can harm data quality and remove suprasegmentals.
Experiments compare LangID, which prepends language-identifying artificial tokens, with NoLangID, using a beam width of 100 to compute error metrics.
The authors use three evaluation metrics.
Phoneme Error Rate (PER) is Levenshtein distance between predicted and gold phoneme sequences divided by gold sequence length.
Word Error Rate (WER) is the percentage of words whose predicted phoneme sequence does not exactly match the gold standard.
Word Error Rate 100 (WER 100) is the percentage of test words whose correct guess is not among the system's first 100 guesses.
For multiple languages, WER, WER 100, and PER numbers are averaged with each language weighted equally.
Phoneme-similarity error metrics would be interesting for multilingual g2p, but are omitted because they have not been widely reported for other g2p systems.
LangID and NoLangID results are compared to deri2016grapheme's system, identified as wFST, whose results have two parts.
High resource results used wFSTs trained on Wiktionary pronunciation data and Wikipedia IPA Help page rules for 85 languages.
Adapted results used mapping strategies for 229 languages, omitting 23 high resource languages with unique scripts or unavailable language distance metrics.
LangID and NoLangID models are each trained on three subsets of the Wiktionary data.
LangID-High and NoLangID-High are trained on data from the 85 languages for which BIBREF13 used non-adapted wFST models.
LangID-Adapted and NoLangID-Adapted are trained on data from 229 languages but actually only 157 languages, omitting 23 High test set languages.
LangID-All and NoLangID-All are trained on data in all 311 languages in the Wiktionary training corpus.
Training was limited to 10,000 words per language, with 10 percent set aside for validation and a maximum of 9000 training words per language.
On 229 languages, LangID outperforms the baseline widely, best with all available languages, while even NoLangID beats the baseline in WER and WER 100.
High resource comparisons use purely monolingual wFST models, and Adapted-trained models are omitted because they performed poorly on unique writing systems like Georgian and Greek.
In High Resource experiments, no sequence-to-sequence approach equals wFST in WER and PER, though LangID models beat wFST in WER 100.
LangID-High is more compact at 15.4 MB, while the combined wFST high resource models are 197.5 MB.
On unseen languages, LangID models have a slight WER and PER advantage, although NoLangID models sometimes do better on WER 100.
Adding a language ID token always improves results when its embedding has been learned, including when the source sequence uses the wrong script, as for Arabic.
Language ID token embeddings are mostly uninterpretable, making unseen-language estimation difficult, so externally constructed typological representations may be more promising.
Phoneme embeddings show many regularities, suggesting the multilingual model learns similar embeddings for phonetically similar phonemes written with the same grapheme.
Phoneme embedding structure may explain strong WER 100 performance, and filtering or reranking system output might improve performance.
Future work could extend language ID token benefits to unseen languages using typological feature tokens from Phoible and WALS to predict orthographic rules.
The artificial token approach could also apply to monolingual English g2p by tagging loanword etymology analogously to language ID in multilingual g2p.
